newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil regrets January trade data confusion.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil regrets January trade data confusion.

text.p: An embarrassed Brazilian government Thursday apologized for confusion over its January trade figures, which were found at the eleventh hour to be missing almost $500 million in oil imports.

Finance Ministry executive secretary Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros sheepishly acknowledged officials had known for weeks that state oil firm Petrobras had not been registering its imports in the brand-new Siscomex computer system.
But he said those low-level officials "did not realize the implications for the trade balance" and for the markets.
"This we regret," Mendonca de Barros said.

Brasilia announced a January trade gap of $413 million, subtracting $473 million in unregistered fuel and lubricant imports from what, until Wednesday morning, had gloriously looked like Brazil's first monthly trade surplus since last May.
The figure cheered some traders and market analysts, who had been expecting fuel imports to be much higher.
"The figure was a positive surprise," said Clive Botelho, executive director at Brazilian investment bank Banco BMG.

The problem with fuel imports had been an inability by Petrobras to adjust to the new Siscomex import registration system, which came on line on January 1, and "bureaucratic" inefficiency at finding a solution.
Mendonca de Barros said that beyond the Petrobras hiccup, there had been no other distortions to imports last month and that the resulting trade deficit was accurate.
He added there would be no further mishaps in the months to come, and that Siscomex and Petrobras were now working faultlessly and perfectly in synch.

"We estimate that January imports were probably about $300 million more than was reported because of problems with Siscomex," said Thomas Malaga, economist at Brazilian retail bank Unibanco. "We see February's trade defict rising to $1.0 billion from $600 million."
The confusion over the trade figures and inept handling of problems with Siscomex led to furious criticism of the government in the media.

"The episode of the January trade balance reveals a scary incompetence in government," wrote columnist Miriam Leitao in O Globo newspaper. "How is possible that the biggest state firm in the country can just ignore the official import system?"
Most private sector trade watchers agree that Siscomex's worst problems, which almost totally barred imports in the first week of January, have been resolved.
But they say small hiccups are likely to continue to occur for at least the first quarter of 1997.

Luiz Furlan, president of meatpackers Sadia and foreign trade representative of Sao Paulo's Fiesp industrial association, defended Siscomex against its critics saying it would eventually guarantee more transparency in trade data.

"This is Brazil," he told Reuters in a recent interview. "Brazilians, by their nature, leave everything to the last minute and that's what happened with Siscomex. People didn't train, they didn't get ready for the new system."
